newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan undecided on air protest at disputed isles.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan undecided on air protest at disputed isles.

text.p: Taiwan government officials told activists on Wednesday to stay calm and exercise self-restraint over the volatile issue of Japan's claim to a deserted archipelago in the East China Sea, state television reported.

Leaders of the private Protect-the-Diaoyus alliance were seeking to rent helicopters to fly on Friday to the uninhabited islands, claimed by Japan as the Senkakus and by Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus.

Activists hoped to drop flags of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government to commemorate Taiwan's October 25 Retrocession Day -- the day in 1945 on which Japan's 50-year occupation of Taiwan ended with Tokyo's World War Two defeat.
The officials had been expected to decide if the activists could fly to the islands but state television said they did not.

"They... asked our countrymen to face the situation with calm and exercise self-restraint," it said. "But the meeting did not make a decision on whether to give a go-ahead for the helicopters to fly to the islands."
The aeronautics administration has said the group needs approval from both Taipei and Tokyo to fly to the Diaoyus since the airspace is jointly controlled by both countries.
Taiwan's foreign ministry, mindful of escalating tensions with Tokyo, expressed "concern" about the planned protest, the state-funded Central News Agency reported.
Two rounds of Japan-Taiwan talks, unofficial because the countries do not have diplomatic ties, have failed to defuse the situation. Japan recognises only the Beijing government, Taiwan's rival.
Foreign minister John Chang said Taipei and Tokyo would hold a third round in Taipei on fishing rights and other issues stemming from the sovereignty row. He did not give a date.
On October 7, Taiwan and Hong Kong activists pierced a Japanese maritime cordon and hoisted flags of the communist People's Republic of China and Taiwan on the islands.
Tokyo voiced regret for what it called the illegal landing and vowed to take necessary measures to stop similar actions.

Japanese rightists triggered an angry and increasingly nationalistic backlash from ethnic Chinese across Asia after raising Japan's flag and building a lighthouse on the islands in July to assert Tokyo's claim.
Taiwan fishermen complain that Japanese patrol boats have barred them from fishing waters near the islands.
The Japanese patrols also repulsed earlier attempts to land Taiwan and Hong Kong protesters on the islands, deepening anti-Japanese resentment in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and the communist mainland.
Japan took the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895 and refuses to acknowledge that the dispute is open for discussion with China or Taiwan.
China and Taiwan say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and should have been returned after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
